t.1.153.1: Janamejaya said: O brahmin, after those tigers among men, the Pāṇḍavas, had thus slain the rākṣasa Baka, what did they do from then on?
t.1.153.2: Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having slain the Rākṣasa Baka, O king, they dwelt right there in the brahmin's house, studying the supreme Brahman.
t.1.153.3: Then, after a few days, a brahmin of rigorous vows came to that house of the brahmin in search of shelter.
t.1.153.4: Then that learned bull among brahmins, who had always vowed to receive every guest, duly honored him and gave him shelter.
t.1.153.5: Then all those Pāṇḍavas, bulls among men, together with Kuntī, sat in attendance upon the brahmin as he told his tales.
t.1.153.7: There, at the end of his tales, O Janamejaya, that brahmin told of the wondrous svayaṃvara of Yājñasenī among the Pāñcālas.
t.1.153.6: He told of lands and of various sacred fords, of the manifold wonders of kings, and of various cities.
t.1.153.8: the birth of Dhṛṣṭadyumna and the birth of Śikhaṇḍin, and how Kṛṣṇā came forth not from a womb at the great sacrifice of Drupada.
t.1.153.10: How did Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the son of Drupada, come forth from the fire, and how did Kṛṣṇā have her wondrous birth from the middle of the altar?
t.1.153.9: Having heard of that most wondrous deed of that great-souled one, unequalled in the world, the bulls among men asked to hear that tale in full detail.
t.1.153.12: Thus urged by those bulls among men, O king, that brahmin then narrated all of it, the birth of Draupadī.
t.1.153.11: How did he learn all the weapons from Droṇa, the great archer? And how did those two dear friends come to be divided, and on whose account?
